questions.enonce_markdown:
2. (a) Determine the inference rule and validity of the following inferences in the Aristotelian system:

(i) All players are liars. So, some non-players are non-liars.

(ii) Some bike riders are farmers. So, All bike riders are farmers. (3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) All players are liars. So, some non-players are non-liars.**

Let $P$ = players, $L$ = liars. The premise is the A proposition *All $P$ are $L$*; the conclusion is the I proposition *Some non-$P$ are non-$L$*.

**Rule: inversion** (the partial inverse of an A proposition, stated with the complementary predicate). It is obtained by a chain of immediate inferences:

| Step | Operation | Result |
|:-:|:-|:-|
| 1 | Obversion | No players are non-liars |
| 2 | Simple conversion (E) | No non-liars are players |
| 3 | Obversion | All non-liars are non-players (the contrapositive) |
| 4 | Conversion by limitation (*per accidens*) | Some non-players are non-liars |

**Validity: valid in the Aristotelian system.** Step 4 (conversion *per accidens*, equivalent to a subalternation) uses **existential import**: the class "non-liars" is assumed to have members. Under that assumption, since every non-liar is a non-player, some non-players are non-liars. (A check over all possible models, with the classes assumed non-empty, finds no counter-model.) The same inference is **invalid in the Boolean system**: if everybody is a liar, "All players are liars" is true but there are no non-liars, so "Some non-players are non-liars" is false.

**(ii) Some bike riders are farmers. So, All bike riders are farmers.**

The premise is an I proposition and the conclusion an A proposition with the same subject and predicate. The inference goes from the **particular to the universal**, which is the reverse of subalternation. The rule of subalternation allows only $A \to I$ and $E \to O$ (from the universal to the particular), never the reverse. This is the fallacy of **illicit superalternation** (illicit inference from the particular to the universal).

**Validity: invalid** in the Aristotelian system (and in the Boolean one). On the traditional square of opposition, when the I proposition is true the A proposition is **undetermined** (doubtful): it can be true or false. Counter-model: some bike riders are farmers and some bike riders are not farmers; the premise is true and the conclusion false.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Using "Agriculturalists" as middle term; "Farmers" as Major term, and "peasants" as minor term

(i) Construct AAI-4 syllogism

(ii) Determine if the syllogism in (b i) above is valid in the Boolean system. Explain your answer. (3 x 2 marks)

(iii) What is the difference between the Boolean and the Aristotelian systems? (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $P$ = farmers (major term), $M$ = agriculturalists (middle term), $S$ = peasants (minor term).

**(i) The AAI-4 syllogism.** In figure 4 the middle term is the **predicate of the major premise** and the **subject of the minor premise**. Mood A-A-I: two universal affirmative premises and a particular affirmative conclusion.

| | Statement | Form |
|:-|:-|:-:|
| Major premise (A) | All farmers are agriculturalists. | All $P$ are $M$ |
| Minor premise (A) | All agriculturalists are peasants. | All $M$ are $S$ |
| Conclusion (I) | Therefore, some peasants are farmers. | Some $S$ are $P$ |

(This is the traditional mood *Bramantip*.)

**(ii) Is it valid in the Boolean system? No.** The two premises are universal and the conclusion is particular. In the Boolean system a universal proposition has **no existential import**: it does not say that its subject class has members. Counter-model: suppose there are **no farmers** (and, if one likes, no agriculturalists and no peasants either). Then "All farmers are agriculturalists" and "All agriculturalists are peasants" are both true (vacuously), but "Some peasants are farmers" is false, since it asserts that at least one peasant exists and is a farmer. The syllogism commits the **existential fallacy**; it is valid only in the Aristotelian system, where the terms are assumed to denote existing things (a check of all models confirms this).

**(iii) The difference between the Boolean and the Aristotelian systems.** The difference lies in **existential import**.

- In the **Aristotelian** (traditional) system, all terms are assumed to denote non-empty classes, so a universal proposition (A, E) implies the corresponding particular (I, O). The whole traditional square of opposition holds (contradictories, contraries, subcontraries, subalternation), conversion and contraposition *per accidens* are valid, and there are **24** valid syllogistic forms.
- In the **Boolean** (modern) system, universal propositions do not assert existence (they mean "if anything is $S$, it is $P$"), whereas particular propositions do. Only the **contradictory** relation survives from the square, subalternation, contrariety and subcontrariety are lost, and **15** syllogistic forms remain valid (those that do not need existential import).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Paraphrase and symbolise the following arguments:

(i) Granted that if men are wise and are rational beings then they are human beings; and that they are wise and rational beings. It follows that they are human beings.

(ii) If Philosophy is the best discipline in life then philosophers practice the virtues preached. But since philosophers do not practice the virtues they preach, one can say that philosophy is not the best discipline in life.

(iii) Either Pastors are good or their Christians cheat. But pastors are good. So, their Christians don't cheat. (3 x 2 marks)

*Alternative For the visually impaired candidates only:* Provide the propositional schema for each of the arguments in b(i-iii) above. (3 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Let $W$ = men are wise; $R$ = men are rational beings; $H$ = men are human beings.

*Paraphrase:* If men are wise and men are rational beings, then they are human beings. Men are wise and rational beings. Therefore, men are human beings.

*Symbolisation:* $(W \cdot R) \supset H,\ \ W \cdot R\ \ \therefore\ H$

Form: *modus ponens* (affirming the antecedent): valid.

**(ii)** Let $B$ = Philosophy is the best discipline in life; $V$ = philosophers practise the virtues they preach.

*Paraphrase:* If Philosophy is the best discipline in life, then philosophers practise the virtues they preach. Philosophers do not practise the virtues they preach. Therefore, Philosophy is not the best discipline in life.

*Symbolisation:* $B \supset V,\ \ \sim V\ \ \therefore\ \sim B$

Form: *modus tollens* (denying the consequent): valid.

**(iii)** Let $G$ = pastors are good; $C$ = their Christians cheat.

*Paraphrase:* Either pastors are good or their Christians cheat. Pastors are good. Therefore, their Christians do not cheat.

*Symbolisation:* $G \vee C,\ \ G\ \ \therefore\ \sim C$

Form: *modus ponendo tollens*; it is valid only if the "either ... or" is exclusive. With the inclusive disjunction of propositional logic it is **invalid** (counter-row: $G$ and $C$ both true).

**Alternative for the visually impaired candidates** ("the arguments in b(i-iii)" can only refer to the three arguments of the present sub-question): the propositional schemata are the three symbolisations above, in letters-free form:

- (i) $(p \cdot q) \supset r,\ \ p \cdot q\ \ \therefore\ r$
- (ii) $p \supset q,\ \ \sim q\ \ \therefore\ \sim p$
- (iii) $p \vee q,\ \ p\ \ \therefore\ \sim q$

(A truth table check: the schemata of (i) and (ii) are valid forms, that of (iii) is not valid with the inclusive "or".)
